subject: mathematics
question_text: If the mth term of an A.P. is 1/n and the nth term is 1/m, show that the (mn)th term is 1.

mark_split.label: Subtract the two equations to find d

steps.label: Subtract the two equations to find d
steps.margin_note: First mark. Combine 1/n − 1/m over the common denominator mn before cancelling. Say m ≠ n before dividing.
steps.memory_tip: 1/n − 1/m = (m − n)/(mn), so the same (m − n) appears on both sides.
lines: Let a be the first term and d the common difference.
Since m ≠ n, divide by (m − n):  d = 1/(mn)

recall.must_convey: That subtracting the two equations gives (m − n)d = (m − n)/(mn), so d = 1/(mn).
accept: subtract the two equations to remove a
one by n minus one by m is m minus n over m n
the common difference is one by m n
rendu subtract cheste d one by m n vasthundi
the m minus n cancels from both sides

steps.why: The right side 1/n − 1/m becomes (m − n)/(mn), and the same factor m − n stands on the left, so it cancels and leaves d directly.
common_mistakes: Writing 1/n − 1/m = (n − m)/(mn) with the subtraction reversed.

steps.label: Find a and the (mn)th term
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Write 1/n as m/(mn) first, so both fractions have the same denominator. a and d come out equal.
steps.memory_tip: a = d = 1/(mn), so the (mn)th term is mn lots of 1/(mn), which is 1.

recall.must_convey: That a = 1/(mn), so the (mn)th term is 1/(mn) + (mn − 1)/(mn) = 1.
accept: the first term is also one by m n
substitute d back to find a
one by m n plus m n minus one by m n is one
a kuda one by m n, so term one avuthundi
a and d are equal so the m n term is one

steps.why: Here a and d both work out to 1/(mn), so the (mn)th term is mn copies of 1/(mn). That is why the answer is exactly 1.
common_mistakes: Assuming a = d without showing it from equation (1).
Writing 1/n as 1/(mn) when putting the two fractions over one denominator.
